source_text:
Fragmentum in epistulam ad Philemonem (in catenis)
Phm
1,1 Ἐν πολλαῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ξένον τίθησι ῥῆμα τοῦ μέλλοντος εἰσάγεσθαι λόγου
κατασκευαστικόν, καὶ νῦν ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλεν ἀξιοῦν ὑπὲρ Ὀνησίμου τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ–
ἀξία δὲ αὐτοῦ τὸ δεδέσθαι–, τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν.
thought_title: Paul's unusual word prepares for his appeal through his chains
orientation: Severianus is explaining how Paul opens the letter to Philemon with a striking word that prepares for the request he is about to make on behalf of Onesimus.
pass_a_gloss: In many letters he places an unusual word, preparatory of the argument about to be introduced, and now since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus by his own worth—and his worth is being in chains—he shows the credibility of the appeal.

choices.why: The glossary specifies 'unusual word' for this key term, and it preserves the rhetorical sense of a striking or unexpected word placed at the start.
The glossary mandates 'preparatory' for this term, which captures the constructive, building-up function of the word toward the coming argument.
The glossary specifies 'make a request' for this verb, which fits the context of Paul petitioning on behalf of Onesimus.
The glossary mandates 'worth' for this noun, which conveys Paul's claim to consideration or dignity.
The glossary specifies 'being in chains' for this perfect infinitive, which emphasizes the state of imprisonment as Paul's worth.
The glossary mandates 'credibility' for this term, which captures the trustworthiness of Paul's appeal.

pass_b_english: In many of his letters Paul places an unusual word at the start, one that is preparatory for the argument he is about to introduce. Here too, since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus, he shows the credibility of his appeal through his own worth—and his worth is being in chains.
